Chapter 7: Hypothesis Testing Pt II

Hypothesis testing for continuous outcomes

One or two samples?

  • One-sample significance tests: is this mean different from some hypothetical value?

  • Two-sample significance tests: are the means of these groups different from one another?

One sample T-Test:

One sample T-Test

I want to know if people are, on average, “warm” towards capitalists. I survey 100 people and get an average feeling thermometer score for “capitalists” was 54.3. Is it plausible that the actual population feeling thermometer score is actually 50 or below?

  • \(H_a\) The average FT for capitalists is greater than 50

  • \(H_0\) The average FT for capitalists is less than or equal to 50

My alpha here is .05, so I’ll reject the null if there’s a less than 5% chance of seeing a result this high if the null is true.

One sample T-Test

Imagine the null is true, then the sampling distribution of sample means would be centered at 50 with a standard error equal to \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

One sample T-Test

Our observed value is 54.3. So, we’re basically asking: what is the probability of getting a result of 54.3 or greater if the population mean is 50?

One sample T-Test: P-value method

  1. Calculate the difference between my observed value and the null value we’re assuming (50)

  2. Calculate the standard error (\(SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\))

  3. Calculate a T-statistic for this difference (\(T = \frac{\text{difference}}{SE}\)) and get the associated p.value

One sample T-Test: P-value method

  1. \(54.3 - 50 = 4.3\) (that part’s easy)

  2. \(s = 25.2\); \(n = 100\). So my standard error = \(\frac{25.2}{\sqrt{100}} \approx 2.5\)

  3. \(T = \frac{4.3}{2.5} \approx 1.7\), (with 99 degrees of freedom)

(Remember that, for large samples, T stats and Z stats will differ very little)

But I can calculate a P-value here if I’m feeling it:

pt(1.7,
   df = 99,
   lower.tail=FALSE # we want to know the probability of getting a T > our observed T if the null is true
   )
[1] 0.04613535

One sample T-Test: P-value method

Note that, if I flip my hypothesis I get a different answer:

\(H_a:\) the population mean is less than 50

\(H_0:\) the population mean greater than or equal to 50

pt(1.7,
   df = 99,
   lower.tail=TRUE # this gives the probability of getting a T < our observed T if the null is true
   )
[1] 0.9538646

One sample T-Test: P-value method

And a two-tailed test will double my p-value:

\(H_a:\) the population mean is not 50

\(H_0:\) the population is 50

pt(1.7,
   df = 99,
   lower.tail=FALSE 
   ) * 2 #we want to know the probability of getting a T score absolutely greater than what we observe
[1] 0.09227071

One sample T-Test Confidence interval method

I could also test this hypothesis using a confidence interval. The two methods are based on the same assumptions, so they which you choose is mostly a matter of preference.

If the confidence range contains the null hypothesis value, then we fail to reject the null at that level.

One sample T-Test Confidence interval method

A p-value of <.05 in a one-tailed test corresponds to a 90% confidence interval. The required T-score at 99 degrees of freedom is 1.67.

\[ 54.3 \pm 1.67 \times 2.5 = [50.13 , 58.5] \]

A p-value of <.05 in a two-tailed test corresponds to a 95% confidence interval. The required T-score at 99 degrees of freedom is 1.98.

\[ 54.3 \pm 1.98 \times 2.5 = [49.34 , 59.25] \]

Two-Sample Test

In a two sample test, I want to know if a pair of estimates are significantly different from one another.

Two-Sample Test

“Right to work” laws prohibit agreements that require employees of a unionized company to pay dues (even if they don’t join a union). States that have right to work laws have lower unionization rates, but is it plausible this difference is the result of random sampling error?

Characteristic
Right to work state?
No
N = 341		 Yes
N = 161
Percent of workers who are union members 11.7 (4.9) 6.1 (2.3)
1 Mean (SD)

Two-Sample Test

For a P-value:

  1. Calculate the difference between the groups.
  2. Calculate the standard error of the difference
  3. Calculate a T-score, and get an associated P-value at the appropriate degrees of freedom.

Two-Sample Test

The difference: \((11.7 - 6.1 = 5.6)\)

To get the standard error of the difference, we need to account for the fact that our estimates of both groups have some error associated with them. So we combine standard errors like this:

\[ SE_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2_{\text{group 1}}}{n_\text{group 1}} + \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{group 2}}}{n_\text{group 2}}} \]

Two-Sample Test

\[ SE_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{\frac{4.9^2}{34} + \frac{2.3^2}{16}} = 1.02 \]

\[ \text{diff} = 11.73 - 6.12 = 5.61 \]

\[ T = \frac{5.61}{1.02} = 5.52 \]

Degrees of freedom here is different depending on your assumptions about the samples, but an okay approximation for our purposes is: \(n_1-1 + n_2-1 = 48\)

Two-Sample Test

The probability of a T-score < 5.61 (at DF = 48):

pt(5.61, df = 48, 
   lower.tail = T) 
[1] 0.9999995

The probability of a T-score > 5.61 (at DF = 48):

pt(5.61, df = 48, 
   lower.tail = F) 
[1] 4.913752e-07

The probability of an absolute T-score >= 5.61 (at DF = 48):

pt(5.61, df = 48, 
   lower.tail = F) * 2
[1] 9.827504e-07

Two-Sample Test: in R

library(RCPA3)
testmeansC(dv = unionized, # the dependent variable
           iv = rtw,       # the independent variable
           data = states  # the data source
          
           )

Cautions about hypothesis testing

How not to use a p-value

How not to use a p-value

  • Charles Cicchetti, writing in a deposition for the plaintiffs in a lawsuit claiming mass vote fraud swung the 2020 election, used a difference of proportion test to compare Biden’s 2020 results in Georgia to Clinton’s results in the same state.

  • The goal was to “test the hypothesis that other things being equal they would have an equal number of votes”

How not to use a p-value

Clinton’s 2016 vote \(= 45.9\%\) with \(4,146,825\) total votes cast

Biden’s 2020 vote \(= 49.5\%\) with \(4,999,960\) total votes cast

\[ \text{diff} = .495 - .459 = .036 \]

\[ \text{SE}_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{\frac{.459 \times (1 - .459)}{4146825} + \frac{.495 \times (1-.495)}{4999960}} = 0.000331 \]

\[ Z = \frac{.036}{0.000331} = 108.7 \]

\[ P |Z| > z \approx 1 \text{ in } 1,000,000,000,000,000 \]

How not to use a p-value

“In my opinion, the outcome of Biden winning is so statistically improbable, that it is not possible to dismiss fraud and biased changes in the ways ballots were processed, validated, and tabulated” - Charles Cicchetti

The math checks out! So what’s wrong with this claim?

What is the null hypothesis in this case? What can we conclude from rejecting it?

How not to use a p-value

if the objective is to assess whether Biden won legitimately, then it is beside the point whether Biden and Clinton enjoyed the same expected support. Support can differ across candidates for any number of reasons, and it is absurd to think that any such difference constitutes evidence of election fraud. -Eggers, Garro, and Grimmer

(the authors go on to note that they can reject this null in every state in every presidential election since 1960)

This tells us that differences across elections aren’t random, but that’s probably not the most important question for researchers!

What hypothesis testing does

In experimental research, “treatment” is randomly assigned, so once we’ve eliminated “random chance”, we can conclude the difference is due to the treatment.

What hypothesis testing does

  • In observational research, ruling out random chance is just the first step towards identifying a cause
  • We’d need to rule out a lot of other more plausible explanations here first.

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

Lots of causes, but bad hypothesis testing plays a role:

  • P < .05 means “1 in 20 results will be a Type I error”

  • So, what happens if I just test everything?

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

Here’s a function that produces random results, runs a t-test, and then determines whether the results are significant at the .05 level:

set.seed(100)

simulate_experiment<-function(){
  N <- 100
  treatment_assignment<-rep(c("control group", "test group"), each = N/2)
  outcome<-rnorm(length(treatment_assignment))
  p<-t.test(outcome ~ treatment_assignment)$p.value
  significance <- ifelse(p < .05, "significant", "not significant")
  return(significance)
}

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

If I run this function 100 times, I’ll get about 5 significant results:

p_values<-replicate(n=100, expr = simulate_experiment())
barplot(table(p_values), main = "Significance tests for 100 simulated experiments")

but there’s definitely not a relationship here. This is random noise!

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

  • The ANES has thousands of variables, so there are bound to be hundreds of combinations that will give us significant results purely by chance.

  • P-hacking, or trying out a bunch of models until one just gets over the threshold for significance, is bound to produce false positives.

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

  • In published research, there are few incentives to publish a non-significant result, so people sometimes run lots of tests and only publish the ones that “work”

  • Which results in lots of findings that later can’t be replicated: they were just random false positives.

Best practices when conducting research

  • Exploring your data is fine (especially when you’re learning) but running more tests means you should be more skeptical of your results.

  • Remember that there’s nothing magical about p<.05. Interpret your p-values and confidence intervals in terms of what they mean about uncertainty, not just in terms of significance/insignificance.

Best practices when reading research

  • As a reader, you should be cautious when you see a result that just barely meets the criteria for significance, especially if its:

    • Not supported by additional replications or the hypothesis wasn’t pre-registered

    • Un-intuitive or not based on some pre-existing theory or reasonable expectation

    • Substantively small and/or based on a small sample

2016 outcome 2020 outcome Z-values in pubished papers in medical research from: van Zwet, Erik W., and Eric A. Cator. “The significance filter, the winner’s curse and the need to shrink.” Statistica Neerlandica 75.4 (2021): 437-452.
